lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: There are no streets in your town. No doors. No windows.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: Wake up! Wake up! The sun is up! Last one on the roof is a sheep!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: I'm coming! Stop shaking the ladder!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: To go outside, you climb a ladder, through a hole in the ceiling. Every single house in town works like this.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Good morning, grandmother.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: Who are you talking to? There's nobody there.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: She's right here. Under my bed.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: And that's true. Your grandmother is buried in the floor, under the platform where you sleep. So is her mother. Here, this is completely normal.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Almost nine thousand years ago, in the middle of today's Turkey, this was one of the biggest towns on Earth. Today we call it Çatalhöyük. And you were born here.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The Konya plain, around six thousand seven hundred BC. Your house has one main room, about five steps wide, and a small storeroom for grain.

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: Don't step there! That's the clean side. Ash and cooking stay by the oven.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Archaeologists found that families kept the messy work, like cooking and making tools, on one side, under the ladder. The other side, with the sleeping platforms, stayed clean.

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: Bring the white clay. The walls need a new coat before the feast.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Again? We did it last month!

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: And we'll do it again next month. Clean walls, happy house.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: Why do we always paint? Nobody ever comes inside.

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: We come inside. And the ancestors are inside.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Some walls here have hundreds of thin layers of white plaster, put on again and again, over many years.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: Can I put my hand on it? While it's still wet?

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: One hand. Red, from the ochre. Just like your father did, when he was little.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: Look! My hand is on the wall forever!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Until mother paints over it next month.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: Hey!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Mother, why are there bull horns in our wall?

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: Those are from the great hunt, before you were born. They watch over us.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Houses here were decorated with the horns and skulls of wild cattle, set into walls and benches. What they meant exactly, nobody knows.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Outside, the town looks like a giant honeycomb. People walk across the rooftops, like streets in the sky.

lines.speaker: NEI
lines.text: Watch your feet! My roof is still wet!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Sorry! Sorry!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Down on the plain, by the river, your family grows wheat, barley, peas and lentils. And you keep sheep and goats.

lines.speaker: FAT
lines.text: Take the sheep to the marsh, and watch for wolves. And don't fall asleep this time.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: That was one time, father!

lines.speaker: FAT
lines.text: One time. And we lost two sheep.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Come on, sheep. Not in the water. Not in the water!

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: A wolf! Over there, in the reeds!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Shout! Throw stones! Make yourself big!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Bread and porridge fed the town. But all that sticky grain was bad for teeth. Many skeletons here have cavities.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: My tooth hurts again.

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: Then stop stealing honey from the neighbours.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That's not a joke, by the way. Traces of beeswax were found in cooking pots from this region, from around this time.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: One day, the hunters come back with big news.

lines.speaker: HUN
lines.text: An aurochs! A giant bull, down by the lake! The biggest any of us has ever seen!

lines.speaker: FAT
lines.text: You're old enough now. Get your spear. Today, you come with us.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Me? Really?

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: Stay behind your father. And come back with both your legs.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The aurochs was the wild ancestor of today's cattle. A big bull could stand almost two meters tall at the shoulder, and weigh about a ton.

lines.speaker: HUN
lines.text: Quiet. Spread out. Wait for my signal.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: It's looking at me. Why is it looking at me?

lines.speaker: FAT
lines.text: Don't move. Let it come to us.

lines.speaker: HUN
lines.text: Now! Spears!

lines.speaker: FAT
lines.text: Run! To the side! Run!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Paintings found in the houses here show crowds of people around giant bulls and deer, some pulling the animal's tail or tongue. Nobody knows if they show real hunts, or stories.

lines.speaker: HUN
lines.text: We did it! Tonight, the whole town eats!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Father, I threw my spear! Did I hit it?

lines.speaker: FAT
lines.text: You hit the ground. Very bravely.

lines.speaker: HUN
lines.text: Ha! Next time, aim for the bull.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: A bull like this could feed hundreds of people. Big feasts may have brought the whole town together. And afterwards, the horns went into the walls.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Your town needs something it can't make itself: obsidian. Black volcanic glass, sharper than any knife.

lines.speaker: TRA
lines.text: Black glass from the fire mountains! The sharpest edge in the world! Who wants it?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: What about that round one? The shiny one?

lines.speaker: TRA
lines.text: That? That's a mirror. Go on. Look into it.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Is that me? That's what my face looks like?

lines.speaker: TRA
lines.text: Two baskets of lentils, and it's yours.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Two baskets? My mother will kill me!

lines.speaker: TRA
lines.text: One basket, and you carry my bags to the edge of town.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Deal!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Polished obsidian mirrors were found in graves here. They are among the oldest mirrors ever discovered.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The obsidian came from volcanoes in Cappadocia, more than a hundred kilometers away. One of them, Hasan Dağı, can be seen from the rooftops on a clear day.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: Look! The mountain! The mountain is on fire!

lines.speaker: FAT
lines.text: Everyone inside! Now! Pull up the ladders!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Scientists have dated an eruption of Hasan Dağı to roughly this time. And one painting found here may show it: a mountain with two peaks, spitting fire, above rows of houses.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Some call it the oldest map in the world. Others say it's just the pattern of a leopard skin. Archaeologists are still arguing.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Life in a crowded town wasn't easy. Several thousand people live packed together, with animals, rubbish, and smoke from every oven.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Why do I cough all the time?

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: Everybody coughs in winter. It's the smoke. Now go and wash your hands.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: In rooms with no windows, people breathed smoke all winter. Archaeologists found black soot on the inside of ribs from burials here.

lines.speaker: NEI
lines.text: That's my roof! You built your wall on my roof!

lines.speaker: FAT
lines.text: Your roof? My grandfather built this wall before you were even born!

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: Enough! Both of you! The elders will decide.

lines.speaker: NEI
lines.text: Fine. But your sister stays off my roof!

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: That was one time!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: And sometimes, people fought. A study in twenty nineteen found healed head wounds on about one in four skulls examined. Many were hit from behind, probably by clay balls thrown with slings.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: But here's something surprising. The bones show that men and women ate the same food, did similar work, and were buried in the same way.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: When I grow up, I want to hunt aurochs, like you.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Then you'll need a bigger spear.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: Then make me one!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: One winter, the old storyteller who lived in your house dies in his sleep. He wasn't your grandfather. He wasn't even related to you by blood.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Where will we put him?

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: Where we put everyone we love. Under the floor. Close to us.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: Can I give him something to take with him?

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: Give him his beads. He loved those beads.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The body is folded tightly, wrapped in cloth or matting, and buried under a platform. Then the floor is plastered smooth again.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: In twenty twenty-one, a DNA study found that many people buried in the same house here were not close relatives. Family was something you made. Not only something you were born into.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: Will he be lonely down there?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: No. He's right under my bed. Now I'll tell him the stories.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Sometimes, the skull of an important person was taken out later, covered with plaster, and painted. One woman was found buried, holding a plastered skull in her arms.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Years pass. You're grown up now. Your house is old, and the walls are cracking.

lines.speaker: FAT
lines.text: It's time. We build the new house.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Where?

lines.speaker: FAT
lines.text: Right here. On top of this one.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: When a house got old, people took off the roof, filled the room with earth, and built a new house on top. Often with the walls in exactly the same place.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Over more than a thousand years, house on house, the town grew into a hill twenty meters high.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: So our old house is under our new house?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: And grandmother's house is under that one. And her grandmother's under that.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That's where the name comes from. In Turkish, höyük means a mound, a hill made by people. Çatal means fork.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Your town lasted more than a thousand years. Then, around six thousand BC, people moved across the river, and later they left for good.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Why? Maybe the climate got drier. Maybe the town was simply too crowded. Nobody knows for sure.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: When I'm old, they'll bury me under this floor too. And one day, someone will build a house on top of me.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: And they'll never know you were here.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Maybe they will.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: In nineteen fifty-eight, a British archaeologist named James Mellaart noticed the mound. In the nineteen sixties, his team found the houses, the paintings, and the bull horns.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: And a little clay figure of a large woman, seated between two big cats. People called her the Mother Goddess.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: For decades, books said the people here worshipped a great goddess, and that women ruled. Today, most archaeologists think that's too simple. Most figurines aren't goddesses at all, and many are animals.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Some of Mellaart's drawings were later questioned too. A few famous wall designs he published were never seen by anyone else.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: But the town itself is very real. Since nineteen ninety-three, teams from around the world have excavated here. In twenty twelve, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Your town is older than Stonehenge, and older than the pyramids of Egypt, by more than four thousand years.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: No streets. No doors. Just ladders, white walls, and the people we loved, under our feet.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: So, could you live here? On the rooftops, in the smoke, sleeping above your ancestors? Tell me in the comments. And if you're ever near Konya, you can still visit it.
